chapter_seo_title: Dao Gui Episode 485: The Dragon Vein Revealed – Ji Lin’s Brutal Inheritance
chapter_meta_description: The Great Liang dragon vein is not a myth—it’s a chained corpse emperor. Ji Lin learns the cost of power in the bleakest succession scene in xianxia horror.
og_title: Dao Gui Chapter 485: The Dragon Vein’s True Face
og_description: Witness the grotesque nature of the Great Liang dynasty’s dragon vein—dead emperors chained and kept alive by parasitic qi.
twitter_title: Dao Gui 485: Imperial Horror at Its Peak
twitter_description: The new emperor Ji Lin must watch his father’s chained corpse give him a lesson in ruthless survival. Dragon veins are not what you think.

lore_anchors.definition: In traditional Chinese geomancy, a flow of beneficial qi along landforms that empowers a dynasty. In the Dao-Twisted World, it is literalized into a chain of dead emperors kept puppet-walking by parasitic dragon qi.
The traditional self-address of the Chinese emperor, meaning “the one who is bereft.” Ji Song’s advice to “trust no one” is a twisted extrapolation of this ancient political principle.
A classical mythic motif often used to transport immortals or celestial emperors. Here, the chains pull inward to restrain rather than escort, inverting the image from honor into imprisonment.
A strong laxative; Ji Lin famously poisoned his brother with these at age six to win favor with his father.
A traditional Chinese term for a lethal toxin (often arsenic), named after the red crown of the red-crowned crane; considered a swift, elegant killing agent.
A fictional sect in the novel fusing Zoroastrianism (袄教) and Nestorian Christianity (景教); Li Huowang’s cover identity claims to be a member.
A powerful court Daoist official with divinatory abilities; Zhuge Yuan’s alias magic prevents him from seeing Li Huowang’s true name.
